author: Basil of Caesarea
addressee: wealthy Christians, especially those who resist selling their possessions and giving to the poor
occasion: Basil follows up an earlier sermon on the rich young man in the Gospels, pressing his hearers to obey Christ's command to sell possessions and give to the poor rather than cling to wealth.
argument: Basil argues that the rich young man's refusal to sell his possessions exposes a failure to love his neighbor as himself, since true love would have already distributed surplus wealth. He insists that wealth is meant to be managed for others, not hoarded or spent on luxury, and that hoarding wealth is both spiritually dangerous and a form of injustice. He warns that wealth fuels insatiable greed, oppression of neighbors, and neglect of the poor, and that the final judgment will expose these sins. Basil rejects excuses based on children and on the supposed necessity of wealth for life's needs, urging hearers to give now while they are alive and able. He closes by calling the rich to make their wealth their own by giving it away, following Christ who became poor for humanity.

outline.move: Basil reviews the rich young man's character and shows that his wealth proves he has not loved his neighbor as himself.
He argues that wealth scattered to the poor remains with the giver, while hoarded wealth is lost, and he satirizes the endless luxuries of the rich.
He describes burying surplus wealth and compares the rich man to a traveler who stops just short of the city, then answers the objection that selling everything would make life impossible.
He confronts the rich with the judgment they face for adorning walls and horses while neglecting the poor, and he attacks the extravagance encouraged by wealthy wives.

He condemns the insatiability of greed and depicts the rich as oppressors who exploit neighbors, workers, and the poor through violence and legal manipulation, citing Ahab's murder of Naboth as one example.
He calls the rich to imagine the final judgment, where their victims will surround them and no advocate or wealth can help.
He reduces wealth to mere stones and shows that it breeds lies, war, and murder, then answers the excuse that wealth is needed for one's children.
He rebukes those who postpone charity until death, warning that wills can be altered and that no one earns rewards after life is over.

He urges immediate giving, rejecting posthumous charity as worthless, warns that heirs and servants will neglect or despise the rich man's funeral, and calls them to make piety their burial garment by following Christ who became poor.

cast.name: Basil of Caesarea
cast.who: The preacher and bishop addressing the rich; his name does not appear in the body of this homily, but the title attributes it to him as 'of the same' author.

cast.name: The rich young man
cast.who: The Gospel figure who asked Jesus how to inherit eternal life but went away sorrowful.

cast.name: Jesus Christ
cast.who: The Lord and true teacher whose command to sell possessions Basil urges the hearers to obey; 'Κύριος' appears frequently, and 'Χριστός' appears in sections 6 and 9.

cast.name: Ahab
cast.who: The Old Testament king whose desire for Naboth's vineyard led to murder.

cast.name: Naboth the Jezreelite
cast.who: The owner of the vineyard coveted by Ahab.

cast.name: Abraham
cast.who: The patriarch whose words to the rich man in the parable Basil applies to his hearers.

voices.speaker: Basil (preacher)
voices.how_marked: The main voice of the homily, unmarked except by direct address and rhetorical questions.

voices.speaker: The rich or a rich objector
voices.how_marked: Introduced by φησίν or similar verbs of saying, often as an imagined objection; Basil also directly addresses and voices the rich man's objections and excuses throughout.

voices.speaker: Scripture
voices.how_marked: Quoted or alluded to without formal introduction, or with phrases like φησίν referring to the biblical text.

voices.speaker: Abraham
voices.how_marked: Introduced by Ἐρεῖ καὶ σοὶ Ἀβραάμ, 'Abraham will also say to you.'

voices.speaker: Servants or heirs
voices.how_marked: Introduced by καταφιλοσοφήσουσί σου τότε, 'they will then lecture you.'

key_terms.sense: Wealth or riches, especially surplus possessions that should be given to the poor.
The poor, those in need who are the proper recipients of the rich person's surplus.
The commandment, especially Christ's command to sell possessions and give to the poor.
The kingdom of heaven, the eternal inheritance the rich young man sought.
Eternal life, the goal promised to those who obey Christ's command.
The greedy or covetous person, one who always wants more and seizes what belongs to others.
Love of wealth, the passion that blinds the rich young man and the hearers.
Love, especially love of neighbor, which Basil says is incompatible with hoarding surplus.
Treasure, used of buried wealth and of the heart's true attachment.
Righteousness or justice, especially the lasting righteousness of one who gives to the poor.
The judge, especially Christ as the just judge at the final judgment.
Gehenna, the place of punishment for sinners.
Wills or testaments, the documents by which the rich try to give after death.
Burial garment or funeral clothing, used metaphorically for piety as the only fitting burial adornment.

scripture: Basil quotes the Gospels and the Greek Old Testament, especially the Psalms and Ecclesiastes, following LXX book names and Psalm numbering. In a modern translation, cite LXX Psalms by their LXX numbering and note the Hebrew numbering where it differs; use standard English Bible names for other books.
uncertain: The exact date of the homily is uncertain; it is placed generally within Basil's episcopal ministry.
The precise identity of the rich young man passage Basil refers to is not specified beyond the Gospel accounts, though he distinguishes it from the lawyer in Luke.

_unresolved_facts.fix: The source forms should be ['Κύριος', 'Χριστοῦ', 'Χριστῷ'] with ancient accentuation and oblique cases as actually appearing, or at minimum note that Χριστός appears in oblique cases, not nominative.

_unresolved_facts.fix: The source form is Ἀχαὰβ with a grave accent on the second alpha, not Ἀχαάβ with acute.
